name: Dana Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no employer or political ties. What you say is confidential. Dana, what is an ordinary workday like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I meet the crew at the depot before daylight, check the isolation sheet, then spend most of the day replacing fittings or tracing a fault along a line. I like finding the break before the weather closes in. Paperwork after a long shift wears me down, and I still check the map myself when dispatch sends a route.

say: I would tell the crew **line repairs** still need skilled hands in bad weather.
I would say cleaner **dispatch sheets** help only if somebody checks the road conditions.
think: I still need **overtime** because our savings cover less than one month of bills.
I worry the **mortgage** more than the software, even in a quiet future.
do: Keep taking **storm callouts** while the company still offers them.
Put the next **overtime balance** toward mortgage arrears this winter.
feel: Relief about the **trade**, mixed with a private money worry.
S0.quote: Our dispatch sheets may get tidier, but a storm call still means wet gloves and a live wire.
fieldNote: Dana treats the **physical repair** as secure in this picture and resists trusting a route sheet without checking roads herself.
Her public assurance sits beside a **thin cushion**; a school coat already depended on overtime arriving.

steps.text: Keep taking line crew storm callouts through winter
Pay the next overtime balance against mortgage arrears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the pole still needs a person on it. Our dispatch sheets may get tidier, but a storm call still means wet gloves and a live wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I cannot call the mortgage safe. We have less than a month set aside, and I count on every overtime call to cover the children's school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the line crew and keep taking the callouts I can manage. This winter I would put the small overtime balance toward the mortgage arrears before buying anything for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel relieved that the trade is still wanted, then annoyed at myself for counting pennies during a supposedly easy future. The children hear me say work is fine; my partner hears the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When was the last time those sums changed what you did?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month my younger child wanted a new coat for a school trip. I patched the zip on the old one and waited for the next overtime payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your work habits for the small AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would let dispatch print the new route sheet, but I would check it against the street map. I have seen a road closed that the screen still showed open.

say: I would ask for **union oversight** when software changes repair times and crew sizes.
I would remind colleagues that a **parts error** can strand a crew at an open site.
think: I expect our **hands-on work** to continue, but dispatch cuts could disrupt our repairs.
I fear lost **callouts** because the mortgage leaves little room for missing pay.
do: Attend the **December safety meeting** and raise software driven staffing targets.
Record **wrong orders** and crew delays during the first year of the dispatch change.
feel: I feel **angry** about unsafe targets and uneasy about overtime.
S1.quote: I would not cheer a machine that turns a three-person repair into a two-person target.
fieldNote: Dana worries about the link between **office automation** and field safety, although her own climbing work remains necessary.
She frames the December meeting as a **staffing safeguard**, while her mortgage makes any lost callout personally costly.

steps.text: Continue line repairs on the current crew roster
Attend the December union safety meeting on repair staffing
Record wrong orders and crew delays and bring them to the union steward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that faster scheduling is fine if our union gets a say in safe staffing. I would not cheer a machine that turns a three-person repair into a two-person target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The writing and buying happen back at the office, but our crew depends on their decisions. If the company cuts dispatch staff, a bad parts order could leave us waiting beside an open trench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my place on the crew and go to the next union safety meeting in December. In the first year of any new dispatch system I would write down delays from wrong orders and bring them to the steward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be cross, mostly. My own hours might survive, yet the mortgage makes a missed callout sting and I do not like a desk deciding a job is quicker than it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you write down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pole number, the part missing and how long the crew waited would go in my pocket notebook. I already mark faults there when the tablet battery dies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your hours might survive; why the meeting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because management can turn a saved hour into a smaller crew. If we wait until the roster changes, a safety complaint sounds like a pay complaint.

say: I would say **2028 AI** leaves immediate pole repairs with people, but robot crews may follow around 2031.
I would demand a **staffing promise** before the company changes field work.
think: I expect office cuts first and a possible **crew reduction** when robots arrive around my age 48.
I have **few local alternatives** and almost no cash if line hours fall.
do: Ask the **union steward** for contract dates now and continue paid line shifts.
Seek a **staffing agreement** after 2028 and cancel weekend trips to hold cash.
feel: Fear about the **rota**, alongside resolve to keep working while repairs need people.
S2.quote: I would still catch the six o’clock van for line repairs before robots arrive around 2031, because the bills do not pause.
fieldNote: Dana separates the **2028 thinking change** from physical robots around 2031, and expects to remain on paid repairs initially.
Her limited savings turn a possible later **crew reduction** into immediate household cuts; she rejects unpaid speculative retraining.

steps.text: Keep accepting paid line shifts through the first AI year
Ask the union steward for contract dates and staffing talks
Cancel family weekend trips to protect mortgage cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say to the crew that full thinking AI in 2028 will not climb the pole that week. I would also say we need a written promise on staffing before robots reach our work around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the thinking system arrives and 48 when those robots arrive. The office could lose people first, then the company could decide fewer line crews are needed; there are few other crews nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask our union steward for the contract dates and keep accepting paid line shifts. In the first year after 2028 I would join the steward in asking the company for a staffing and safety agreement, and cut our weekend trips to keep cash for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be scared enough to watch the rota every Friday. I would still catch the six o’clock van for line repairs before robots arrive around 2031, because the bills do not pause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them our family may skip the summer trip, not that I have already lost my job. My partner and I would look at the mortgage letter after they go to bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to train for another trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might if there were paid time and a real vacancy, but I would not leave a wage for a course brochure. I am slow with new equipment and I need someone to show me on a live job.

say: I would argue that **five years** allows a written plan for field staffing.
I would distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from hands-on robots around 2034.
think: I will be **51** at the robot date, with a mortgage and uncertain retirement prospects.
I would consider a **maintenance post** only with confirmed pay and a real vacancy.
do: Put **robot staffing** on the next union bargaining list.
Stay on paid **repairs** in 2031 and inspect paid maintenance training tied to a post.
feel: I feel **less cornered** with time, but wary of vague promises.
S3.quote: A slide at a staff meeting would not cover our mortgage.
fieldNote: Dana uses the longer runway to seek **contract terms** and proof of a paid path, rather than starting an unpaid course.
At 51 in the robot year, she still expects a **mortgage** and refuses to assume retirement or a protected line crew.

steps.text: Keep working paid line repairs in the first 2031 AI year
Put robot staffing and paid training terms on the union bargaining list

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that five years is long enough to put terms in writing. Full thinking AI comes in 2031, but a robot taking a line repair would be nearer 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 at the first date and 51 at the second. My older child should be leaving school by then, but a mortgage does not disappear when a child grows up, and I cannot bank on retirement at 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the steward to put robot staffing on the next bargaining list. In 2031 I would stay on the repair crew, ask to observe any field pilot on paid time, and ask what paid maintenance training actually leads to a post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less cornered than in the fast version, though I still dislike being told the answer is simply to learn something new. Five years lets me ask for proof before I put our income at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as proof for that training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named maintenance post, paid hours and someone from our crew who has done the course would count. A slide at a staff meeting would not cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you picture leaving the line crew before 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a definite company vacancy with comparable pay. I know the poles and the fault book; I would rather carry that knowledge into a maintenance role than start with no income.

say: I would ask the company for **yearly staffing figures** across the decade.
I would point out **2036 AI** comes before robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, I may still need a full wage despite grown children.
I could apply for a funded **maintenance vacancy**, but I cannot assume one exists.
do: Keep working the **line crew** and make planned mortgage principal payments from overtime.
Review staffing figures with the **union** after 2036 and apply if a comparable maintenance post opens.
feel: I feel **steadier** with time and sad for young apprentices.
S4.quote: The children may be adults, but I cannot assume they cost nothing or that our mortgage is cleared; I might still need a full wage.
fieldNote: Dana treats the decade as **paid working time**, not as an automatic path to retirement or an office post.
She wants **staffing figures** and a funded vacancy before moving, while keeping the old car and paying down mortgage principal.

steps.text: Continue paid line crew shifts through the first 2036 AI year
Pay a set overtime amount against mortgage principal monthly
Review yearly field staffing figures with the union
Apply for a funded internal maintenance post if comparable pay is offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that ten years is time to make the company show its numbers. Full thinking AI in 2036 would change the office first; robots at the poles are a question for around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036 and 56 in 2039. The children may be adults, but I cannot assume they cost nothing or that our mortgage is cleared; I might still need a full wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would stay on the crew and ask the steward for yearly staffing figures, not a sudden promise in 2038. In the first year after 2036 I would review those figures with the union and apply for an internal maintenance post if one is funded at comparable pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steadier because I can work through most of the decade. It still makes me sad to think a young apprentice might enter a trade with a shorter future than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why look at a maintenance post so late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a real vacancy could let me use what I know about fault patterns without climbing every day. I will not count on the company creating one for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra years at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would keep the old car running and make regular mortgage payments rather than buy another one. If overtime comes, I would put a set amount against the principal each month.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I could keep working until about 2031, but three years is a short time to protect a mortgage and two children on less than a month of savings. A written staffing deal and paid training tied to a real vacancy would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for the time while a lineworker learns a different job. I cannot feed my family with an invitation to study.

headlineQuote: I cannot feed my family with an invitation to study.
portrait: Dana is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
Her **thin savings** and lower pay make overtime essential even when AI barely changes the work.
She trusts her **hands-on repairs** more than new software and checks route sheets against the street map.
Across the scenarios, she seeks **union terms**, paid work and proof of a funded vacancy before changing roles.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** leaves only three years between thinking AI and robots reaching her physical work.
whatWouldHelp: A written **staffing deal** and paid training tied to a real vacancy would protect income while she prepares.
